item.content:encoded:
The Colorado Rockies are 57–99.
Purple Row After Dark: If the Rockies could steal one player
An absurd rule for absurd times: if the worst team in baseball could steal one player from a playoff club, who should the Rockies take?
One more loss will give them their fourth consecutive 100-loss season, and they are almost certainly going to finish with the worst record in baseball.
These are absurd times for the Rockies, so I have devised an appropriately absurd rule to help them out.
The team with the worst record in baseball gets to steal one player from a playoff team.
There are, naturally, some restrictions. We’re freezing the playoff field as it stood before games on Sunday, September 20. The player has to come from one of those 12 teams, cannot be a pending free agent, and you cannot take the player who leads his team in FanGraphs WAR. The Rockies also inherit the player’s existing contract.
No, one player is not suddenly turning the Rockies into a contender. But could one poached superstar at least keep this thing from becoming five consecutive 100-loss seasons?
Here’s the board:
| Team | Off limits: fWAR leader | Highest available fWAR | Other players worth considering |
| Rays | Junior Caminero (5.2) | Drew Rasmussen (4.7) | Jonathan Aranda (3) |
| Guardians | Parker Messick (4.6) | Steven Kwan (3.4) | Gavin Williams (3.4), Brayan Rocchio (3.3), José Ramírez (2.2) |
| Rangers | Ezequiel Duran (4.6) | Jacob deGrom (4.2) | Josh Jung (2.9), Wyatt Langford (2.8) |
| Yankees | Cam Schlittler (6.1) | Ben Rice (4) | Cody Bellinger (3.9), Aaron Judge (2) |
| Red Sox | Willson Contreras (4.1) | Payton Tolle (4) | Ceddanne Rafaela (3.9), Ranger Suárez (3.7) |
| White Sox | Miguel Vargas (5) | Chase Meidroth (4) | Tristan Peters (3.9), Sean Burke (3.1) |
| Brewers | Jacob Misiorowski (6.3) | Brice Turang (5.4) | Jackson Chourio (4), Jake Bauers (3.6) |
| Dodgers | Shohei Ohtani (6.7) | Yoshinobu Yamamoto (4.7) | Max Muncy (4.3), Andy Pages (3.9) |
| Braves | Chris Sale (5.7) | Michael Harris II (4) | Matt Olson (4), Drake Baldwin (3.1) |
| Cubs | Pete Crow-Armstrong (10.2) | Alex Bregman (5) | Dansby Swanson (3.6) |
| Padres | Fernando Tatis Jr. (5) | Jackson Merrill (4) | Ty France (3.8), Mason Miller (3.7) |
| Phillies | Cristopher Sánchez (5.8) | Jesús Luzardo (5.6) | Zack Wheeler (3.5), Bryce Harper (3.4) |
For me, the choice comes down to Brice Turang, Yoshinobu Yamamoto and Aaron Judge.
Turang is probably the sensible choice.
At 5.4 fWAR, he would easily lead the Rockies, giving them a legitimate top-end player while immediately solving second base for the foreseeable future. He’s 26, hitting .266/.367/.441 with an .808 OPS, and brings value on both sides of the ball with elite range, strong baserunning and a 95th-percentile walk rate.
It would be a very easy way to make the roster better.
But the Rockies really need starting pitching.
Enter Yoshinobu Yamamoto.
He’s 14–8 with a 2.51 ERA, 178 strikeouts and a 0.87 WHIP over 179 innings. His Statcast profile is just as impressive: 100th-percentile pitching run value, 99th-percentile fastball run value, 95th-percentile offspeed run value and a 91st-percentile xERA.
Pitchers are risky, and Yamamoto comes with a lot of money attached. But it’s hard to argue with either the profile or the results, and the addition of the Penner family makes absorbing that contract a lot easier to imagine.
Speaking of high-priced items...
Aaron Judge.
Judge being available is basically a loophole created by our own stupid rule. Injuries have limited him to just 285 plate appearances, which is why he sits at only 2 fWAR, but he’s still hitting .241/.360/.511 with 15 home runs.
And the underlying numbers are still very much Judge: a .396 xwOBA, .569 xSLG, 94.0 mph average exit velocity and a 57.5% hard-hit rate.
It is very hard to look at that and say, “No thanks.”
After all, Aaron Judge is the type of hitter that, if he were playing 81 games a year at Coors Field, I might take out a small loan for season tickets.
So who are you stealing?

item.title: [New York Post] Dodgers considering Emmet Sheehan for playoff role after gem in win over Giants
item.dc:creator: Dylan Hernandez
item.description: Emmet Sheehan’s next start will be in the minor leagues. The right-hander might be out of sight, but that doesn’t mean he will be out of mind. His scheduled start Saturday for triple-A Oklahoma City in a Pacific Coast League playoff game is part of a design to prepare him to pitch for the Dodgers in October. item.content:encoded:
Emmet Sheehan’s next start will be in the minor leagues.
The right-hander might be out of sight, but that doesn’t mean he will be out of mind.
His scheduled start Saturday for triple-A Oklahoma City in a Pacific Coast League playoff game is part of a design to prepare him to pitch for the Dodgers in October.
Sheehan has pitched his way into consideration for a spot on the playoff roster.
His quote-unquote demotion came after he pitched 5 ⅓ scoreless innings in the Los Angeles Dodgers’ sweep-sealing 3–1 victory over the San Francisco Giants Sunday.
The game was the third Sheehan pitched this month for the Dodgers. His numbers in those three games: 17 innings pitched, one run allowed, 24 strikeouts, three walks.
“I’ve loved the version we’ve seen of Emmet the last three outings,” manager Dave Roberts said. “He’s been fantastic.”
Sent down to Oklahoma City in early August, Sheehan returned to the major leagues earlier this month with a slightly modified arsenal that has significantly improved his results. He’s thrown his curveball more, and his increased inability to change speeds has made his fastball play up even when he’s not touching 97 mph with it.
“I think that obviously there’s a 97 that plays better, but 94–95 commanded still misses bats,” Roberts said. “So I think that’s something that, that’s one part of it. The other part of it is holding the velocity. And so, for me, the last three or four since he’s been back here, he’s held those 94s and 95s for the, call it, 85 pitches.”
With the Dodgers expecting to start Yoshinobu Yamamoto, Blake Snell, Tarik Skubal and Tyler Glasnow in the postseason, the team has started the process of moving Sheehan into a relief role by having Jack Dreyer pitch an inning as opener Sunday. Sheehan was down in triple-A over the last week but a roster spot for him was opened up because Skubal went on the bereavement list.
Sheehan entered the game in the second inning and pitched into the seventh. He gave up only one hit and one walk; he struck out nine.
He said he has made it a point to feel “free and easy” with his delivery.
“Instead of saying, ‘I need 97 [mph] here,’ it’s more like, ‘If I hit my spot, he’s not going to hit it,’” Sheehan said.
What it means
The teams with the two-best records in each league will earn a first-round bye and the Dodgers are close to wrapping up one of those spots. With their win over the Giants, the Dodgers maintained a four-game lead over the Atlanta Braves for the National League’s No. 2 seed. Both teams have only six games remaining in the regular season.
Who’s hot
Left-hander Kris Bubic, who was acquired from the Kansas City Royals at the trade deadline, replaced Sheehan in the seventh inning and registered the final two outs of the inning. Bubic struck out Scott Bandura, only for Shay Whitcomb to reach base on a throwing error by Max Muncy.
No problem: Bubic forced Grant McCray to fly out to left field.
Bubic has pitched 2 ⅔ innings in three appearances for the Dodgers over the last week, and he still hasn’t allowed a run. He has struck out four.
Roberts said he’s also pitched his way into consideration for a spot on the playoff roster.
“It’s nothing overpowering, but there’s just funky swings, soft contact,” Roberts said. “I see him as a neutral pitcher, gets left and right out, and I like those converted starters because he knows how to navigate lineups.”
Who’s Not
For today, this section should be renamed “Who Wasn’t Hot.”
The label certainly applied to Tommy Edman, who was two for his last 42 before his sixth-inning at-bat: That’s when Edman jumped on an inside cutter from Carson Seymour and launched it into the visiting bullpen behind the right-field wall.
Edman’s home run tied the game at 1–1.
Up next
The Dodgers have a day off Monday. They will resume play Tuesday when they host the San Diego Padres, who will send No. 1 starter Michael King (12-9, 3.03 ERA) to the mound. The Dodgers won’t have a traditional starter, as Roberts said the team is planning for a bullpen game.

item.title: [Dodgers Nation] Roki Sasaki Heading Back to Dodgers' Bullpen With Postseason Looming
item.dc:creator: Aaron Coloma
item.description: The Los Angeles Dodgers will move right-hander Roki Sasaki to the bullpen when he returns from the injured list in their next series against the San Diego Padres. Sasaki, 24, landed on the injured list at the end of August, putting an end to a dominant run which came after the All-Star break. Why Would the Dodgers Move Roki Sasaki to a Relief
item.content:encoded:
The Los Angeles Dodgers will move right-hander Roki Sasaki to the bullpen when he returns from the injured list in their next series against the San Diego Padres.
Sasaki, 24, landed on the injured list at the end of August, putting an end to a dominant run which came after the All-Star break. He allowed two runs or fewer in each of his appearances leading into an Aug. 26 start against the Atlanta Braves, during which he allowed four earned runs.
Why Would the Dodgers Move Roki Sasaki to a Relief Role?
The Dodgers have to trim their rotation to four players when the postseason comes, so putting Sasaki back into the bullpen is only natural given the other players they have on their roster.
Tyler Glasnow, Tarik Skubal, Blake Snell and Yoshinobu Yamamoto are all likely to remain starters, so Sasaki’s relief role isn’t especially surprising. Roberts revealed Sasaki could operate in slightly different situations upon his return, potentially handling several innings in relief.
“I could see multiple innings but it’s not gonna be bulk like 4 or 5 innings,” Roberts said, per Dodgers Nation’s Noel Sanchez.
“…I trust Roki in any situation. [His first appearance] won’t be in the ninth the first time. It could potentially fall out, but it won’t be that way.”
Sasaki has the stuff to be a high-leverage reliever and showed he was more than capable last season. His fastball ranks among the fastest in MLB, topping out above 100 mph, and his limited arsenal suggests he’ll see even more success as a reliever.
How Did Roki Sasaki Perform Out of the Bullpen Last Season?
Sasaki returned from a long-term stint on the injured list towards the latter end of last season. He made two appearances before the end of the year as a reliever, holding opponents scoreless in both before entering the postseason in the same role.
The right-hander looked like a brand new pitcher in the postseason, making nine appearances and only allowing one earned run through 10.2 innings pitched.
He took over as the team’s closer during their postseason run, and went 3-for-3 in save opportunities throughout October.
The Dodgers will hope he can find that same form in the bullpen this year as they chase a historic three-peat.

item.content:encoded:
LOS ÁNGELES -- El dicho asegura que el pitcheo gana campeonatos, y eso fue cierto de distintas maneras cuando los Dodgers conquistaron Series Mundiales consecutivas en 2024 y 2025.
Los Dodgers de 2024 tuvieron que apoyarse mucho en su bullpen por necesidad, mientras que el equipo de 2025 se respaldó en su rotación para defender con éxito el título, a tal punto que sus cuatro abridores lanzaron en el decisivo Juego 7.
Mientras los Dodgers buscan un tricampeonato este año, volverán a depender de sus cuatro abridores, Yoshinobu Yamamoto, Tarik Skubal, Blake Snell y Tyler Glasnow, para marcar la pauta. Pero su bullpen parece menos inestable que el año pasado y podría ser uno de los grupos con mayor flexibilidad mientras Los Ángeles evalúa cómo conformar sus rosters para la postemporada.
Los Dodgers pudieron observar a varios candidatos para el bullpen de playoffs al ejecutar con éxito un juego de bullpen la tarde del domingo en el Dodger Stadium, completando una barrida de tres encuentros sobre los Gigantes con una victoria por 3-1. El derecho Emmet Sheehan ponchó a nueve en 5.1 innings en blanco como relevista largo, dándole a Los Ángeles otra interesante alternativa para la postemporada.
La cuarta victoria consecutiva de los Dodgers mantuvo su ventaja de cuatro juegos sobre los Bravos por el segundo mejor récord de la Liga Nacional, y el descanso en la primera ronda de la postemporada que viene con esa posición, cuando restan seis juegos por disputar.

item.title: [MLB.com] How Sheehan, Sasaki and others look to fit in LA's postseason 'pen plans

The 2024 Dodgers had to lean heavily on their bullpen out of necessity, while the '25 team rode its rotation to a successful title defense -- so much so that all four starting pitchers took the ball in the winner-take-all Game 7. item.content:encoded:
LOS ANGELES -- The saying goes that pitching wins championships, and that was true in different ways when the Dodgers won back-to-back World Series in 2024 and '25.
The 2024 Dodgers had to lean heavily on their bullpen out of necessity, while the '25 team rode its rotation to a successful title defense -- so much so that all four starting pitchers took the ball in the winner-take-all Game 7.
As the Dodgers go for a three-peat this year, they'll once again look for their starting four of Yoshinobu Yamamoto, Tarik Skubal, Blake Snell and Tyler Glasnow to set the tone. But their bullpen feels less volatile than it was last year, and it could be one of the most fluid position groups as L.A. considers how to piece together its postseason rosters.
One way or another, the Dodgers will carry their best 13 pitchers in the postseason, because as manager Dave Roberts has said repeatedly, like a mantra: "Every inning in the postseason is leverage."
The Dodgers got a look at several postseason 'pen candidates when they ran a bullpen game to success on Sunday afternoon at Dodger Stadium, capping a three-game sweep of the Giants with a 3-1 victory. Right-hander Emmet Sheehan struck out nine in 5 1/3 scoreless innings of bulk relief, giving L.A. an intriguing option to add to the mix.
The Dodgers' fourth straight victory maintained their four-game lead over the Braves for the second-best record in the National League -- and a first-round postseason bye -- with six games left to play.
The greatest need in the bullpen is right-handed leverage arms. Edwin Díaz, who signed a three-year, $69 million deal to be their closer, has been relegated to lower leverage for the time being amid his poor performance in an injury-ravaged season. Edgardo Henriquez, who stepped up to become L.A.'s most reliable righty in leverage, is out for the rest of the regular season due to a lower back strain. He could return during the postseason, but the uncertainty still creates a need.
Evan Phillips and Brock Stewart have been solid options, but they have been more valuable as part of the bridge to the ninth inning, rather than to close out games. In order to find such options from the right-hand side, the Dodgers can turn to the strength of their staff: the rotation.
Sheehan is one candidate, although he'll remain stretched out through the end of the regular season as rotation depth. Another is Roki Sasaki, who was also originally going to remain built up as a starter upon his return from the 15-day IL. Instead, Roberts said, Sasaki will likely be activated Tuesday and be available out of the bullpen, beginning his transition to relief in the final days of the regular season.
"He's done it. He's really good. He's a neutral pitcher, high-octane stuff," Roberts said. "You really just need four starters, you know. So we're in a good spot there for now."
Sheehan and Sasaki both got a crash course in short-burst relief last fall. While Sasaki thrived as the Dodgers' postseason closer, Sheehan was scored on in his first four appearances before rebounding for scoreless outings in Games 3 and 7 of the World Series.
For Sheehan, adapting his typical routine to relief was difficult, but he believes that he can build on last year if he gets the call to the 'pen again.
"Having that experience helps a lot," Sheehan said. "Just getting back into that, I know what I need to do to get ready to go into the game."
And don't count out Díaz. His pitch to earn a spot in the postseason 'pen began with two scoreless innings against the Giants this weekend.
When the postseason comes, the Dodgers may not be able to avoid using Díaz in leverage, even if they don't throw him into a comparable situation in the final days of the regular season. But if he shows enough this week, then L.A. will bet on his track record.
"I gotta show them I’m part of that bullpen," Díaz said. "I haven’t pitched [much] this year, and when I’ve been on the mound I’ve been struggling. So right now, I’m giving my 200% just to show them I will be in that roster spot."

item.title: [True Blue LA] Better late than never: Dodgers offense pounces on the Giants’ bullpen in win
item.dc:creator: Estevão Maximo
item.description: Repeating the trend of these series’ first two games, the Dodgers didn’t take the lead until the second half of the game—this time keeping their scoring to nearly the minimum needed to overcome the Giants, sweeping their rivals with a 3-1 victory that relied heavily on Emmet Sheehan’s work as the bulk man, following Jack Dreyer. Better late than never: Dodgers offense pounces on the Giants’ bullpen in win Emmet Sheehan’s outstanding work as a follower allowed the Dodgers to beat the Giants with
item.content:encoded:
Repeating the trend of these series’ first two games, the Dodgers didn’t take the lead until the second half of the game—this time keeping their scoring to nearly the minimum needed to overcome the Giants, sweeping their rivals with a 3-1 victory that relied heavily on Emmet Sheehan’s work as the bulk man, following Jack Dreyer.
Better late than never: Dodgers offense pounces on the Giants’ bullpen in win
Emmet Sheehan’s outstanding work as a follower allowed the Dodgers to beat the Giants with just three runs
Without putting the ball in play, the Giants placed a man on third in the opening inning, manufacturing a run partially thanks to Dreyer’s loose grip on the running game. Leadoff hitter Jonah Cox earned a walk as Dreyer struggled to locate his heater, moved to second on an errant pickoff attempt, and aggressively stole third—hardly a surprise for a rookie with 13 stolen bases in just 140 plate appearances. Cox was driven in by a Jonah Bericoto single, a run that would loom large given the effectiveness of both Sheehan and Giants starter Matt Wilkinson.
Deceptive with his low-90s fastball that gets terrific results, Giants starter Matt Wilkinson didn’t encounter many problems holding the Dodgers scoreless through five innings of work. Only twice did Wilkinson need to strand one-out doubles, but on both occasions with minimal stress. That success was at least partially owed to a lefty-heavy lineup—three of the four outs Wilkinson recorded with a runner in scoring position came against a left-handed hitter, but then again, one of the doubles came from Josue De Paula, so we mustn’t read too much into it.
As soon as Wilkinson got the hook, though, the Dodgers would tie the game in the bottom of the sixth, thanks to a solo shot from Tommy Edman off Carson Seymour. Traditionally a better power hitter from the right side, Edman was looking in the whole way and crushed one all the way out to the Giants’ bullpen.
The only reason why the Dodgers were able to tie the score with just one swing was the fact that Sheehan matched Wilkinson pitch for pitch and then some. Overall, few players have improved their case for a significant postseason role over the past couple of weeks with the Dodgers quite like Sheehan, a new pitcher since his return following a one-month stint in Triple-A. Pitching as brilliantly as he did in two September starts, Sheehan completely shut down the Giants’ lineup through 5.1 innings, enjoying great success with a curveball that induced six whiffs on 12 swings, leading him to strike out nine batters.
Proving Wilkinson and his difficult-to-pick-up fastball were the problem, the Dodgers’ offense scored again in the seventh—they took the lead thanks to a Kiké Hernández RBI single after De Paula and Max Muncy set the table despite an unfavorable matchup against the southpaw.
Mookie Betts nearly put this game to bed, but what would’ve been a two-out, three-run bomb died at the wall, leaving the score at 2-1. The Dodgers would still find a way to provide a little cushion to Tanner Scott in the ninth inning, adding one more run in the bottom of the eighth thanks to a Max Muncy two-out RBI single.
Game particulars
- Home run— Tommy Edman (7)
- WP—Kris Bubic (4-2): 0.2 IP, 1 strikeout
- LP— Sam Hentges (1-7): 0.1 IP, 3 hits, 1 run
- SV Tanner Scott (23): 1 IP, 1 walk, 1 strikeout
Up next
It’s a rare off day at home for the Dodgers before the San Diego Padres come into town on Tuesday hoping to clinch their playoff berth. Although neither team has announced their starters, based on the current schedule, the first game of that series would pit Yoshinobu Yamamoto and Robbie Ray against each other. It’s a standard 7:10 p.m. (PT).

item.content:encoded:
Dodgers pitcher Tarik Skubal is going on the bereavement list, manager Dave Roberts announced on Sunday.
The move came a day after Skubal suffered his worst start with the Dodgers, giving up four runs in five innings in Saturday’s 10-4 win over the San Francisco Giants.
In his absence, Emmet Sheehan was called up from triple-A, returning in hopes of building off back-to-back strong starts earlier this month. He will follow opener Jack Dreyer on Sunday as the bulk pitcher for the Dodgers’ series finale with the Giants.
Roberts said Skubal would be away from the Dodgers for “a couple days.” No further information on his situation was available.
Skubal is a contender to be the Dodgers’ Game 1 starter in the playoffs, after being acquired in a blockbuster deal at the trade deadline in August. Even after Saturday’s setback, in which he allowed eight hits and bemoaned his lack of fastball command, the left-hander is 4-2 with a 2.95 ERA in nine starts with the Dodgers this season.
The two-time Cy Young Award winner will anchor a postseason rotation also expected to include Yoshinobu Yamamoto, Tyler Glasnow and Blake Snell (assuming he continues to recover from his recent groin injury).
The Dodgers also freshened up their bullpen on Sunday, swapping out right-handers was calling up Kyle Hurt and optioning Seth Halvorsen.
The team enters Sunday with the chance to not only sweep the Giants, but further lower their current magic number of four to secure a first-round bye in the playoffs.
They enter play on Sunday four games ahead of the Atlanta Braves for the No. 2 seed in the National League.

item.title: [Dodgers Way] One stat defines just how dominant Yoshinobu Yamamoto has been for Dodgers
item.dc:creator: Evan Roberts

item.content:encoded:
The Los Angeles Dodgers starting rotation is so good collectively when they are healthy that it's sometimes difficult to focus on the individuals' accomplishments.
As a fan, it's easy to just look at the starting unit of Yoshinobu Yamamoto, Tarik Skubal, Blake Snell, Tyler Glasnow, and Shohei Ohtani as one. But Yamamoto's latest feat stands out even relative to this dominant group of pitchers.
Dodgers starter Yoshinobu Yamamoto has been dominant this season
Yamamoto's most recent start came on September 15 against the Cincinnati Reds at Great American Ball Park. It was yet another ho-hum performance by the Dodgers ace. He picked up the win going seven scoreless innings, while allowing just one hit. He only walked two batters while striking out seven. Yamamoto lowered his career WHIP to 0.96, which is officially the best WHIP ever by a pitcher their first 75 career starts.
Yamamoto outpaced 2025 National League Cy Young Award-winner — and perhaps future Dodgers pitcher in Paul Skenes — as well as former member of LA's pitching staff, Walker Buehler. Behind Yamamoto, Skenes, and Buehler are Seattle Mariners All-Star starter Bryan Woo and Tampa Bay Rays right-hander Drew Rasmussen.
Not only does Yamamoto have the best WHIP ever through his first 75 games, but he's allowed the third-fewest runs in MLB history by a pitcher through that same span (trailing only Rasmussen and Skenes).
Opposing hitters are hitting .192/.252/.310 against Yamamoto through those 75 starts -- that is the lowest batting average against of any pitcher since 1974 (when that data became available). It's also the lowest on-base percentage, the fifth-lowest slugging percentage, and the second-lowest OPS.
Below is a list of fewest hits allowed in MLB history by a pitcher in their first 75 starts. There's a lot of familiar names on that list.
| Pitcher | Hits Allowed |
|---|---|
| 1. Tony Gonsolin (LAD) | 264 |
| 2. Freddy Peralta (MIL) | 270 |
| 3. Drew Rasmussen (TB) | 284 |
| T-4. Cristian Javier (HOU) | 287 |
| T-4. Edward Cabrera (MIA) | 287 |
| 6. Triston McKenzie (CLE) | 295 |
| 7. Jack Flaherty (STL) | 299 |
| T-8. Yoshinobu Yamamoto (LAD) | 305 |
| T-8. Shohei Ohtani (LAA) | 305 |
| 10. Tyler Glasnow (LAD) | 313 |
Yamamoto has clearly been worth every penny since he signed that mega-deal with the Dodgers. It's nice to be able to point to his historic regular season success as well as his historic postseason success. Yamamoto is slowly building up a Hall of Fame résumé through his first three Major League seasons.

item.title: [Just Baseball] Is Blake Snell the Dodgers’ Best Pitcher Right Now? | Just Baseball
item.dc:creator: Ryan Murphy
item.description: The Los Angeles Dodgers have done it again. With the Dodgers’ win on Thursday afternoon, they officially clinched the NL West championship for the fifth consecutive year. This marks the Dodgers’ 13th NL West title out of the past 14 years, with their lone second place finish coming in 2021 behind an otherworldly season from the San Francisco Giants. item.content:encoded:
The Los Angeles Dodgers have done it again.
With the Dodgers’ win on Thursday afternoon, they officially clinched the NL West championship for the fifth consecutive year. This marks the Dodgers’ 13th NL West title out of the past 14 years, with their lone second place finish coming in 2021 behind an otherworldly season from the San Francisco Giants.
It has been an interesting season for this Dodgers team. After a scorching hot 56-30 start through June, the Dodgers slumped to a 26-25 record in July and August. Now hunting for the top seed in the National League for the postseason, the Dodgers have bounced back to an 11-5 record in September (as of Thursday).
A major factor in the Dodgers’ volatility this year has been their susceptibility to injury. This year alone, a whopping 27 players have seen time on the Dodgers’ injured list.
The majority of these players have made their way back from the injured list, to varying degrees of success. Of those who have returned to the active roster, one player stands above them all.
Starter Blake Snell has been on a tear since his return from the injured list. While his status moving forward is now in question following his early exit from his September 16 start against the Cincinnati Reds, his run of dominance has been a sight to behold.
Yet, for Snell, the journey to get to this point has been far from a walk in the park.
Stats as of September 17.
Celebrations and Setbacks
Snell came into the 2026 season as arguably the co-ace of the Dodgers’ starting rotation, alongside Yoshinobu Yamamoto.
The left-hander had been a pivotal part of the Dodgers’ 2025 World Series run, allowing just two runs over his first 21 innings of work. Snell cooled off significantly in the World Series, allowing 10 earned runs over 13 innings, but he was invaluable to the Dodgers nonetheless.
However, Snell’s heavy usage in October had some untoward downstream effects. Left with minimal recovery time between the end of the season and the beginning of spring training, Snell had difficulty getting ramped back up for the year. As a result, his offseason throwing progression suffered unanticipated delays.
Lingering shoulder fatigue kept Snell off of the mound through early May, missing the first 38 games. Finally, nearly a month and a half into the 2026 season, Snell was set to make his season debut. Unfortunately for Snell and the Dodgers, his return was interrupted almost immediately.
After three innings against the Atlanta Braves on May 9, Snell’s season debut was done. He allowed four earned runs, striking out five batters while allowing six hits and two walks. Unbeknownst to Snell, this would be his last start for over three months.
Snell was scratched from his next scheduled start. Just one day later, he underwent surgery to remove loose bodies from his left elbow. As a result, Snell missed another 78 games, finally making his return in early August. Since then, he seems to have unlocked a new level.
Second-Half Hero
Snell has long been known to elevate his game during the second half of each season. For his career, he has posted a 3.96 ERA in the first half and a 2.31 ERA during the latter half. As good as his career second-half numbers may be, he’s been even better in his return to the mound this year.
Over his last seven starts, Snell has pitched to an incredible 1.01 ERA, recording 47 strikeouts and 14 walks over 35.2 innings. Opponents are batting a measly .164/.254/.205 against him, and he has allowed no more than one run in any start during this span.
With a sample this small, it is difficult to quantify just how effective Snell has been compared to his Dodgers teammates. This is especially true given the run their starting rotation has been on in recent weeks.
Both Yamamoto and the Dodgers’ marquee trade deadline pickup, Tarik Skubal, have been dominant in their own right. Since Snell returned to the rotation on August 11, Yamamoto and Skubal have each posted an ERA under 2.10 over 30+ innings apiece.
Still, Snell’s ERA over the same span clears both of theirs by a full run. Though Skubal narrowly edges out Snell in fWAR (1.8 fWAR vs. 1.7 fWAR), Snell’s success is all the more unprecedented given this is his first sustained stretch of play since the 2025 postseason.
Expanding beyond just the Dodgers, Snell’s metrics stack up well among the league’s best. Among all qualified pitchers over the same span, Snell holds the second-best ERA, third-best FIP, second-best fWAR, and third-best K/9 rate. He is the only qualified pitcher to have yet to surrender a home run over this span.
What’s Been Working?
Since returning from the IL, Snell has demonstrated a number of improvements.
For one, his stuff seems to have jumped in effectiveness. Every one of Snell’s pitches has seen either a marginal or significant jump in induced movement.
In particular, his fastball has gained nearly an inch of both induced vertical break and horizontal break. This pairs incredibly well with his improved curveball, which has gained two inches of depth and over an inch of horizontal movement.
Factoring in his slider and changeup, Snell’s arsenal has looked remarkably effective as a whole. As a result, his two best pitches have played up in a big way. Though the sample is small, Snell’s fastball has allowed just a 5.6% hard-hit percentage. While batters hit .309 and slugged .426 against his heater in 2025, those figures have dropped to .179 and .232 so far this year.
The results on his curveball have been even more effective, as batters are batting and slugging .086 against it. In 37 plate appearances, hitters have recorded just three hits against Snell’s curveball compared to 20 strikeouts. He has yet to allow an extra-base hit with his curveball in 2026.
Beyond Snell’s improved arsenal, he has also located the ball well. A pitcher with Snell’s profile traditionally operates best working around the edges of the strike zone. This allows him to induce whiffs and chase swings, leading to a higher strikeout rate and more frequent weak contact, but also more walks.
Snell has leaned into this philosophy, attacking early while working around the edges later in at-bats. He has thrown fewer balls in the zone overall, improving his chase rate, but has also significantly increased his first-pitch strike percentage.
Room for Concern
Snell’s run of dominance has been impressive, to say the least. But, his most recent start brings a sobering point to the conversation around his performance.
Last year, the Dodgers leaned heavily on Snell at the end of the regular season and the postseason. He did not bounce back gracefully, missing over 100 games in the 2026 season.
This year, the Dodgers hope to lean on Snell heavily once again as they approach October baseball. As such, it is reasonable to air concerns around the volatility of his health, with his most recent start as an example.
Snell left after one inning against the Reds, citing a left groin issue. In years past, Snell has missed anywhere from a few weeks to a couple of months battling the same issue.
However, he did frame his decision to exit the game as precautionary, rather than reactive. According to Snell, he felt the area tighten up during his pre-game bullpen, and he felt it was best not to push it. While he still hopes to make his next start, nobody can know for sure what the full impact of this issue will wind up being.
The Dodgers have yet to make any further announcements around the injury. At this time, Snell has not been placed on the injured list either. The first real test will be whether Snell ends up making his next start. Manager Dave Roberts has weighed the idea of delaying it, but any deviation from the norm will have an impact at this stage.
Whether Snell remains healthy through October is anybody’s guess. Regardless, his remarkable performance since coming back from injury is a testament to both his talent and resilience. Hopefully, fans can look forward to Snell making a comeback against the San Diego Padres next week.

item.title: [True Blue LA] The growing Dodgers 10-strikeout club
item.dc:creator: Eric Stephen
item.description: Tyler Glasnow on Friday night struck out 10 Giants in his six innings, his most in a start this season. Aside from securing Los Angeles-area folks a free Jumbo Jack with a purchase of a large drink for the 130th time this season and the 27th time in the last 28 days, Friday affirmed the Dodgers’ unique spot in double-digit strikeout games this season. The Dodgers now have a dozen individual 10-strikeout games this season. That’s not the most, it’s tied for fourth-most with the Toronto Blue Jays,
item.content:encoded:
Tyler Glasnow on Friday night struck out 10 Giants in his six innings, his most in a start this season. Aside from securing Los Angeles-area folks a free Jumbo Jack with a purchase of a large drink for the 130th time this season and the 27th time in the last 28 days, Friday affirmed the Dodgers’ unique spot in double-digit strikeout games this season.
The Dodgers now have a dozen individual 10-strikeout games this season. That’s not the most, it’s tied for fourth-most with the Toronto Blue Jays, behind the Milwaukee Brewers (16), Cleveland Guardians (15), and Philadelphia Phillies (14).
But what makes the Dodgers unique this season is that eight different pitchers have achieved double-digit strikeouts in a game:
- Yoshinobu Yamamoto (May 31, July 4, September 9)
- Emmet Sheehan (April 24, September 7)
- Blake Snell (August 11, August 29)
- Shohei Ohtani (April 15)
- Roki Sasaki (June 5)
- Justin Wrobleski (June 30)
- Tarik Skubal (August 22)
- Tyler Glasnow (September 18)
The next-closest team is the Minnesota Twins, with five different pitchers striking out at least 10 in a game this season. The Houston Astros, Brewers, New York Yankees, Pittsburgh Pirates, Texas Rangers, and Seattle Mariners have four pitchers each.
The Dodgers have eight different pitchers, which is at least one measure of their depth.
Eight pitchers with 10 strikeouts is the most the Dodgers have ever had in a season, two more than in 2022.
Saturday game info
- Teams: Dodgers vs. Giants
- Ballpark: Dodger Stadium
- Start time: 6:10 p.m.
- TV: SportsNet LA, MLB Network (out of market)
- Radio: AM 570 (English), KTNQ 1020 AM (Spanish)

item.content:encoded:
Dodgers esperan que Snell (ingle) haga una apertura más antes de la postemporada
This browser does not support the video element.
LOS ÁNGELES -- Dos días después de salir de su apertura tras apenas una entrada debido a rigidez en la ingle izquierda, Blake Snell lanzó desde 90 pies de distancia en el terreno del Dodger Stadium antes del primer juego de la serie del viernes contra los Gigantes. Salió sintiéndose bien, y los Dodgers creen que evitaron lo peor con una lesión que ha sido un problema recurrente a lo largo de la carrera del zurdo.
"Feliz de que lo detectamos a tiempo", indicó el manager Dave Roberts, quien señaló que Snell no fue enviado a hacerse ninguna prueba de imagen.
Los Dodgers se mantienen optimistas de que el dos veces ganador del Premio Cy Young hará otra apertura en la temporada regular en algún momento durante sus nueve juegos restantes. El día específico está por verse -- su turno regular en la rotación caería durante la serie de tres choques de Los Ángeles ante San Diego que comienza el martes -- pero no se espera que lance con ninguna limitación.
"Creo que sería más una apertura normal", aseguró Roberts. "Tal vez no lo exijamos muchísimo, dado que no sabemos cómo se desarrollará la temporada. Pero esta será su última salida de la temporada regular, así que creo que sería más una apertura regular".
This browser does not support the video element.
Snell inició la campaña en la lista de lesionados de 15 días con fatiga en el hombro izquierdo, haciendo su debut de temporada apenas el 9 de mayo. Casi de inmediato volvió a la lista de lesionados debido a cuerpos libres en su codo izquierdo, los cuales fueron removidos mediante el procedimiento NanoNeedle Scope. Desde que regresó el 11 de agosto, Snell ha lucido como si no hubiera perdido el ritmo, registrando efectividad de 1.01 en siete aperturas, con 47 ponches y 14 bases por bolas en 35.2 entradas.
Para un lanzador que comparte la rotación con Yoshinobu Yamamoto y Tarik Skubal, Snell es una pieza absolutamente vital en los planes de los Dodgers para los playoffs. Si su condición empeora, la profundidad del pitcheo abridor de Los Ángeles de repente luce bastante mermada. Está Tyler Glasnow, quien abrió el viernes contra San Francisco pero que ha lidiado con sus propios problemas de lesiones este año. También se espera que Roki Sasaki (fuera desde el 27 de agosto por una ampolla en el dedo medio derecho) regrese pronto para una última apertura en la temporada regular.
Dada la historia de Snell de lanzar bien luego de largas ausencias de acción en Grandes Ligas, ¿han considerado los Dodgers permitirle saltarse su próxima apertura, que siga descansando y esperar a que vuelva a la loma una vez que comiencen los juegos de postemporada?
"Se ha pensado en eso", reveló Roberts. "Pero todavía estás hablando de unos posibles 17 días, algo así... es mucho tiempo para no estar en competencia. Donde normalmente, con su historial, todavía tienes rehabilitaciones y cosas por el estilo. Así que no es sólo cuestión de conectarlo y ya, que descanse dos semanas y lance en un juego de playoffs".

item.title: [Los Angeles Times] Commentary: Dodgers have no choice. They must hope Tyler Glasnow can trust himself in the playoffs
item.dc:creator: Mirjam Swanson
item.description: - Click here to listen to this article - - The oft-injured Tyler Glasnow hasn’t had the greatest of seasons, but the Dodgers will need him to deliver in the playoffs if they want to win another World Series title. - Glasnow fought through early struggles to throw six innings and strike out 10 in an 8-2 win over the San Francisco Giants, but can he replicate that in the playoffs? - The veteran right-hander played a key role in the Dodgers’ 2025 World Series, and the team will need him to do
item.content:encoded:
- Click here to listen to this article
-
- The oft-injured Tyler Glasnow hasn’t had the greatest of seasons, but the Dodgers will need him to deliver in the playoffs if they want to win another World Series title.
- Glasnow fought through early struggles to throw six innings and strike out 10 in an 8-2 win over the San Francisco Giants, but can he replicate that in the playoffs?
- The veteran right-hander played a key role in the Dodgers’ 2025 World Series, and the team will need him to do the same this October.
The Dodgers are all in, going for a three-peat.
And they might not have an extra ace up their sleeve anymore, but when the postseason begins, they’ll still hope to play their quad of aces — four of a kind that will beat almost every other hand.
But do the Dodgers have four aces? Or three? Or just a pair, Yoshinobu Yamamoto and Tarik Skubal?
Could the left groin tightness that chased Blake Snell from his last start after an inning linger into the postseason? Snell isn’t the sturdiest of starters, having missed most of the season because of shoulder fatigue and loose bodies in his left elbow. But the Dodgers suggest he’s going to be OK; Snell is slated for one last regular-season start.
And what about Tyler Glasnow?
Tyler Glasnow gives up just three hits and strikes out 10, and Mookie Betts hits two home runs in the Dodgers’ 8-2 win over the San Francisco Giants.
Can the Dodgers trust the 6-foot-8 right-hander who missed three months because of back spasms?
Should they put their belief in the 11th-year pitcher who likely would be the odd man out in the postseason if Shohei Ohtani still were available to deal on the mound?
They’re going to have to trust Glasnow. And he’s going to have to trust himself.
“He’s a guy that you can’t put too much thought into him, or it starts getting in his own head,” said catcher Dalton Rushing, who is injured but enjoyed watching Glasnow find his footing in Friday’s 8-2 victory over the San Francisco Giants.
“It was a lot of fun to watch tonight,” Rushing said. “Looked like himself.”
After three suboptimal innings, Glasnow settled down in a trust-building exercise of an outing against the Giants and their triple A-caliber lineup.
He wasn’t the most efficient, the most pristine, the sharpest — but he was fit to throw 98 pitches and six innings.
To fight through after laboring with 59 pitches in the first three innings, to earn his second win since April and to help the Dodgers maintain their four-game buffer over the Atlanta Braves as they play to secure a first-round bye with eight games left.
There was no champagne hangover for Glasnow on Friday — he flew directly back to L.A. from Miami, skipping Thursday’s clubhouse party in Cincinnati, where the Dodgers celebrated clinching the National League West Division for the 13th time in 14 years — but how about a toast to good health?
Cheers to giving up just two runs, one each in the second and third innings. To walking only two batters and striking out 10. To giving up only three hard hits and producing 15 whiffs.
To feeling and pitching better.
“After that third inning, I just stopped trying to be quick,” Glasnow said. “Just go out and be athletic, and I think it started to feel a little bit more timed up.”
Glasnow came into Friday’s game — one of his final two regular-season starts — having given up eight runs on 11 hits and seven walks in his previous two starts, looking less than comfortable in both. Out of rhythm, out of sync.
“This is an important start, and he knows it,” manager Dave Roberts said before the game. “It’s certainly not do or die, but ... just to kind of get back feeling good.”
Afterward, Roberts wasn’t thrilled with how Glasnow started, but liked how he finished.
“You could see him fighting himself a little bit,” Roberts said. “The fastball command wasn’t great early. Got a lot of strikeouts. Curveball wasn’t sharp. But I thought he did a good job of making pitches when he needed to. The slider got better, fastball command got better as the game went on. Good to see him get through six innings.”
It’ll be better yet for the Dodgers’ odds if Glasnow can carry Friday’s progress into his next start — and then into the playoffs, where he proved himself as a Dodger last season after an elbow sprain sidelined him for the 2024 postseason.
The magic is indeed missing, and after two seasons of conjuring up postseason greatness, these back-to-reality Dodgers appear headed for an early fall.
In the Dodgers’ 2025 World Series run, Glasnow made six appearances, three of them starts. He had a 1.69 ERA and averaged 10.5 strikeouts per nine innings. The stuff of aces.
“Today was a step in the right direction,” said Glasnow, the formerHart High School star, before leaving the clubhouse in flip-flops. “I’d rather kind of feel it, work through some stuff, and have a good one right before playoffs.
“I think I’m in a good spot right now.”

item.content:encoded:
シーズンを通して先発ローテーションを守り抜き、ドジャースのナ・リーグ地区優勝に貢献した山本由伸投手。鉄腕エースを巡り、米メディア『CLUTCH POINTS』は18日（日本時間19日）、「もっと注目されるべき」と訴えた。なぜ、過小評価されているのか。同メディアはその理由に言及した。
■「活躍が見過ごされている」
今季のドジャース先発投手陣は、ブレイク・スネル投手、タイラー・グラスノー投手が序盤から戦列を離れ、終盤を迎えて大谷翔平投手も負傷者リスト（IL）に入った。
エース格が不在となる中、ひとり先発ローテーションを守ったのが山本だった。今季27試合に先発登板し、14勝8敗。防御率2.51はメジャー全体5位、WHIP（1イニングあたりの被安打と与四球）は0.87で同2位、被打率.180は同3位につけている。
堂々たる成績だが、ナ・リーグのサイ・ヤング賞争いはジェイコブ・ミジオロウスキー投手（ブルワーズ）が先行。これにクリス・セール投手（ブレーブス）やクリストファー・サンチェス投手（フィリーズ）らの名前が続く。
この状況を歯がゆく感じているのが、『CLUTCH POINTS』のジョーイ・ミストレッタ記者。「ミジオロウスキーらの傑出したパフォーマンスにより、山本の活躍が見過ごされている」と指摘。その上で「過小評価されているとまでは言わないが、一番問題なのは（ロサンゼルスという）巨大市場を本拠地とするチームでプレーしているにもかかわらず、彼に向けられる注目が十分ではないということだ」と憤った。
■全体17位の奪三振数が影響か
同記者は注目度が高まらない理由について、「目を見張るような三振を奪っているわけではないからかもしれない」と推察。「山本はここまで178奪三振を記録しており、この時期としては立派な数字。しかし、リーグ全体では17位にとどまっている」と紹介した。
現在は最速104マイル（約167キロ）の剛速球を投げるミジオロウスキーが243奪三振でリーグトップに立ち、ブルージェイズのディラン・シース投手（236奪三振）、ガーディアンズのギャビン・ウィリアムズ投手（235奪三振）が全体の2、3位につけている。
同記者としては、山本が剛腕タイプではなく、制球力重視のスタイルであることが、成績に見合うだけの注目を得られない一因かもしれないと指摘した形だ。
また、同記者は「ドジャースには大谷をはじめ多くのスター選手が在籍しており、たとえ山本のような優秀な選手であっても見過ごされる傾向にある」とも主張した。
その上で、最後に「山本がサイ・ヤング賞を受賞することは難しいかもしれない。しかし、彼は現在受けている評価以上に注目されるべき存在であることは確かだ」と説いた。

item.title: [MLB.com] Snell (groin) expected to start again for Dodgers before postseason
item.dc:creator: Sarah Wexler

item.content:encoded:
LOS ANGELES -- Two days after he exited a start following just one inning due to left groin tightness, Blake Snell threw from 90 feet on the field at Dodger Stadium prior to Friday’s series opener against the Giants. He emerged feeling good, with the Dodgers believing they avoided the worst with an injury that’s been a recurring issue throughout the left-hander’s career.
“Happy that we caught it early,” said manager Dave Roberts, who noted that Snell was not sent to receive any imaging.
The Dodgers remain optimistic that the two-time Cy Young Award winner will make another regular-season start sometime during their remaining nine games. The specific day is to be determined -- his regular spot in the rotation would come up during L.A.’s three-game series vs. San Diego that begins on Tuesday -- but he is not expected to pitch with any limitations.
“I think it'd be more of a normal start,” said Roberts. “Maybe not pushing him a ton, given that we don't know how the season's going to play out. But this will be his last regular-season start, so I think it'd be more of a regular start.”
Snell began the season on the 15-day injured list with left shoulder fatigue, not making his season debut until May 9. He almost immediately went back on the IL due to loose bodies in his left elbow, which were removed using the NanoNeedle Scope procedure. Since returning on Aug. 11, Snell has looked like he hasn’t missed a beat, pitching to a 1.01 ERA over seven starts, with 47 strikeouts and 14 walks in 35 2/3 innings.
For a pitcher who shares a rotation with Yoshinobu Yamamoto and Tarik Skubal, Snell is an absolutely vital part of the Dodgers’ postseason rotation plans. Should his condition worsen, the Dodgers’ starting pitching depth suddenly looks pretty thin. There’s Tyler Glasnow, who started on Friday against San Francisco but has dealt with injury issues of his own this year. Roki Sasaki (out since Aug. 27 with a right middle finger blister) is also expected to return soon for one final regular-season start.
Given Snell’s history of pitching well following long layoffs from Major League action, have the Dodgers given any consideration to letting him skip his next start, continuing to rest and waiting to have him pitch again once postseason games get underway?
“There is a thought,” said Roberts. “But you're still talking about a potential 17 days, something like that -- that's a long time to not be in competition. Where typically, with his history, you still have rehabs and things like that. So it's just not kind of a plug-and-play, sit it out for two weeks and pitch in a playoff game.”

item.title: [Yahoo Sports] Dodgers hopeful to avoid worst-case scenario with injured star pitcher
item.dc:creator: Jack Harris
item.description: So far, so good in Blake Snell's bid to make another start before the end of the regular season. Despite leaving his last outing on Wednesday in Cincinnati after just one inning due to tightness in his left groin, Snell arrived at Dodger Stadium on Friday already feeling better, saying his groin was back up to an "8 out of 10" before heading out for a session of flat-ground catch play in the outfield. item.content:encoded:
So far, so good in Blake Snell's bid to make another start before the end of the regular season.
Despite leaving his last outing on Wednesday in Cincinnati after just one inning due to tightness in his left groin, Snell arrived at Dodger Stadium on Friday already feeling better, saying his groin was back up to an "8 out of 10" before heading out for a session of flat-ground catch play in the outfield.
Dodgers manager Dave Roberts also offered an optimistic outlook on Snell's status, saying he was "very hopeful" in the left-hander's chances to get back on the mound before the beginning of the playoffs.
"Happy that we caught it early," Roberts said of Snell's injury.
Indeed, when Snell exited Wednesday's game after 19 pitches, it raised immediate concerns about the state of the Dodgers' rotation.
Given the injuries the team is dealing with in its bullpen and its offense's inconsistent form through the second half of the season, the Dodgers will almost certainly need to lean on their starters during the playoffs — similar to the way they did last year, when a rotation of Snell, Yoshinobu Yamamoto, Tyler Glasnow and Shohei Ohtani (who will effectively be replaced by Tarik Skubal this year) carried the pitching staff to a second consecutive World Series title.
Losing Snell — who was already sidelined for three months earlier this season following an elbow procedure and has a history of left groin injuries throughout his career — would have dealt a massive blow to those plans.
However, the Dodgers are at least initially optimistic they've avoided anything close to a worst-case scenario.
While Roberts acknowledged that there is still "a little bit of uncertainty" regarding Snell, and no exact date for when he might pitch again, the skipper also noted that the two-time Cy Young Award winner didn't require medical imaging; another sign of the team's confidence that his injury was not more severe.
It's possible that, even if Snell continues to feel better, the Dodgers could elect to rest him for the remainder of the regular season to ensure he doesn't suffer any further setbacks before the playoffs.
But, they are also wary of giving Snell too long of a layoff entering the postseason.
"It's not just kind of plug-and-play," Roberts said, "[to] sit it out for two weeks and pitch in a playoff game."
Thus, the team will continue to monitor Snell's progress in the coming days, hopeful that a potential pitching crisis has been averted.
"We feel confident," Roberts said.

item.title: [DodgersBeat] Dodgers Temper Stone, Miller Expectations
item.dc:creator: Los Royers
item.description: ATLANTA, GA — Gavin Stone and Bobby Miller delivered encouraging performances during their rehabilitation assignments this week, but Los Angeles Dodgers manager Dave Roberts tempered expectations that either right-hander is close to claiming a significant role in the major-league pitching staff. Their performance
item.content:encoded:
ATLANTA, GA — Gavin Stone and Bobby Miller delivered encouraging performances during their rehabilitation assignments this week, but Los Angeles Dodgers manager Dave Roberts tempered expectations that either right-hander is close to claiming a significant role in the major-league pitching staff.
Stone threw four scoreless innings for Triple-A Oklahoma City, allowing one hit and striking out five. Miller followed with three scoreless innings, one hit allowed and five strikeouts. Their performances naturally raised questions about whether the Dodgers could use either pitcher during the final month of the regular season.
Roberts said both pitchers are progressing, but described their immediate value to the organization in one word.
“Right now, to be quite honest, I think it’s depth,” Roberts said.
Dodgers Temper Expectations for Stone and Miller
The Dodgers entered the season hoping Stone and Miller could eventually strengthen their pitching options, but injuries have prevented both from building a normal workload.
Stone has spent the entire season on the injured list with right shoulder inflammation after missing all of 2025 while recovering from shoulder surgery. He began his rehab assignment with Oklahoma City on August 6 and made his fourth appearance Wednesday.
The right-hander threw 58 pitches, including 41 strikes, and retired the final 10 batters he faced. It was his strongest performance since beginning the assignment and represented another positive step in a comeback that has required considerable patience.
Miller has been on the 60-day injured list all season because of right shoulder soreness. He began his Oklahoma City rehab assignment on August 5 and threw 49 pitches, including 33 strikes, during his three-inning outing Wednesday.
“They’re both doing well. They’re both coming back,” Roberts said. “But I think right now, to be quite honest, I think it’s depth.”
Health and Workload Remain the Priority
Roberts explained that both pitchers have experienced abbreviated seasons without enough competitive innings to immediately be considered finished products.
“Both those guys have had a very abbreviated season, not a lot of competitive baseball,” Roberts said. “And where we’re at on the calendar, I think it’s just getting these guys back to healthy and taking down starts or outings and sustaining that, which they both haven’t done in quite some time.”
That does not eliminate the possibility that Stone or Miller could contribute if the Dodgers need another arm. It does show that the organization is prioritizing their long-term recovery over forcing either pitcher into an immediate role because of one strong outing.
The Dodgers currently have a crowded rotation that includes Yoshinobu Yamamoto, Tarik Skubal, Blake Snell, Tyler Glasnow and Roki Sasaki. Shohei Ohtani is also nearing a return to game action, while Eric Lauer is available to provide length from the bullpen.
That depth gives Los Angeles the flexibility to let Stone and Miller continue rebuilding without rushing them. Roberts had previously discussed Stone as a possible multi-inning bullpen option down the stretch, but his latest comments indicate Stone must first prove he can sustain his workload.
Strong Rehab Outings Still Matter
Roberts’ caution should not erase the progress both pitchers have made. Stone and Miller returned to game action earlier this month after extended absences, giving the Dodgers two additional options who were unavailable for most of the season.
Their long-awaited returns to competitive pitching were important steps by themselves. Their latest results offer more evidence that the rehabilitation process is moving in the right direction.
For now, however, the Dodgers are viewing both starters as insurance rather than building their stretch-run plans around them. Stone and Miller must continue taking down innings, recovering well between appearances and showing that their shoulders can handle a consistent schedule.
If they accomplish that, the Dodgers could revisit their roles. Until then, their strongest contribution may be providing organizational depth while positioning themselves to enter next season healthy.

item.title: [heavy.com] Dodgers Provide Roki Sasaki Insight Ahead of Return From Injury
item.dc:creator: Toran Flores
item.description: The Los Angeles Dodgers have faced multiple injury scares in the pitching rotation. Still, they remain focused on preparing for a third straight World Series win. One question about the Dodgers’ pitching centers on right-hander Roki Sasaki. The 24-year-old has been sidelined since revealing a blister on his throwing hand. He is eyeing a return before the postseason, although his role in Los Angeles’ rotation remains unknown. Learning of Blake Snell’s recent groin injury has forced the Dodgers to
item.content:encoded:
The Los Angeles Dodgers have faced multiple injury scares in the pitching rotation. Still, they remain focused on preparing for a third straight World Series win.
One question about the Dodgers’ pitching centers on right-hander Roki Sasaki. The 24-year-old has been sidelined since revealing a blister on his throwing hand. He is eyeing a return before the postseason, although his role in Los Angeles’ rotation remains unknown.
Learning of Blake Snell’s recent groin injury has forced the Dodgers to pivot to a new strategy.
“To be safe, the Dodgers are likely to keep building up Roki Sasaki as a starter,” wrote The Athletic’s Katie Woo. “Sasaki threw a four-inning simulated game Wednesday in Cincinnati. While the Dodgers would prefer to use Sasaki in relief in the postseason, keeping him stretched out on a starter’s workload is smart insurance as they await further developments with Snell.”
Roki Sasaki’s Success as a Postseason Relief Pitcher
While struggling in his first year with the Dodgers in 2025, the team moved Roki Sasaki to a relief role during the postseason. This change worked out well for Los Angeles on its path to a World Series win.
Through nine appearances during the 2025 postseason, Sasaki finished with a 0.84 ERA, 1.03 WHIP, three saves, and two holds. He allowed just one earned run across his postseason run.
Sasaki transitioned into 2026 with similar struggled as the year prior. In 23 starts this season, the second-year starter has a 5-5 record, 4.60 ERA, and 1.33 WHIP across 119.1 innings pitched.
Los Angeles is preparing to have a stacked postseason rotation. It includes 2025 World Series MVP Yoshinobu Yamamoto, Tarik Skubal, Blake Snell, and Tyler Glasnow.
Dodgers Are Closing in on a First-Round Bye
With a little over a week left of the MLB regular season, the Dodgers have their eyes set on clinching a first-round bye in the postseason. Earlier this week, Los Angeles earned the NL West title.
Now, finishing as a top-two team in the National League will secure a top seed and a much-needed break before their postseason run. Entering Friday, the Dodgers hold a four-game lead over the Atlanta Braves for the No. 2 seed.
The top position in the NL is also very much on the table. The Milwaukee Brewers currently own the spot, but hold just a two-game lead over the Dodgers.
It will definitely be something to monitor heading into the weekend. Los Angeles faces the San Francisco Giants in two separate series and the San Diego Padres to finish out their regular season.

item.dc:creator: Conor Liguori

item.content:encoded:
Why Dodgers' top rookie of 2026 is not Josue De Paula originally appeared on The Sporting News. Add The Sporting News as a Preferred Source by clicking here.
The Los Angeles Dodgers have no shortage of talent.
Even with Shohei Ohtani on the injured list, the NL West club has one of, if not the best, rosters in the Majors.
Concerns about the bullpen are warranted. But a starting three in the rotation of Yoshinobu Yamamoto, Tarik Skubal, and one of Blake Snell, Tyler Glasnow, and Justin Wrobleski is dominant.
With Ohtani on the IL, the Dodgers promoted a new talented prospect to replace him at designated hitter: slugger Josue De Paula.
De Paula promptly hit a homer just a few games into his first taste of the Majors and has a .789 OPS through 25 plate appearances.
But Bleacher Report's Kerry Miller believes it's too soon to label him the best Dodgers rookie of the season. Instead, Miller awarded that distinction to a middle infielder.
"There's already a case to be made for Josue De Paula in this spot, even though he just made his MLB debut as Shohei Ohtani's fill-in last Friday," Miller wrote.
"However, [Alex] Freeland spent much of the season as the Dodgers' primary second baseman, providing decent value with his glove while hitting just well enough to earn regular playing time."
Freeland doesn't have eye-popping offensive numbers, hitting .230 with four home runs and a 79 OPS+.
But he has +3 outs above average while playing at three infield spots, mainly second base.
De Paula could change Miller's mind during the final week of the regular season. Manager Dave Roberts should give him plenty of playing time.
For now, Freeland has done enough to warrant the title as the Dodgers' best rookie of the year.

item.title: [sports.yahoo.com] Kyle Tucker’s flirtation with history gives Dodgers more hope of turnaround

item.description: Welcome to the California Post's weekly Dodgers recap, where we review the week that was, hand out very official awards and take stock of the state of the season. item.content:encoded:
Welcome to the California Post's weekly Dodgers recap, where we review the week that was, hand out very official awards and take stock of the state of the season.
PLAYER OF THE WEEK
Kyle Tucker (12-for-29 since Sept. 9; triple shy of the cycle on Thursday)
Off the bat, it appeared history was afoot.
Already on Thursday afternoon, Kyle Tucker had kicked his slow late-season turnaround into a suddenly more hopeful gear, hitting a two-run home run in the first, an RBI double in the second and a single that aided a three-run rally in the fourth.
Now, standing at the plate just a triple shy of the cycle in the eighth, he laced a line drive that made the feat feel possible.
With yet another squared-up swing, the $240 million slugger shot a ball into the left-center field gap. As two Reds outfielders converged on it, the entire Dodgers dugout rose in anticipation.
Alas, the 11th cycle in Dodgers history would have to wait.
The Reds turned a clean relay play. Tucker wisely — although, somewhat disappointingly, given the lopsided score — pulled up at second. And on the bench, all his teammates could do was razz him by mimicking send signs with their arms helplessly waving.
"I tried my best, but I don't think I was gonna get there," he told SportsNet LA afterward. "I probably would've been thrown out halfway."
Oh, well.
For this year's Dodgers, Tucker's 4-for-5, three-RBI game was still hugely encouraging, continuing what is now a weeklong surge in which the four-time All-Star has finally looked like himself.
Even before this stretch, the Dodgers committed to keeping Tucker as a key part of their lineup.
They hoped a breakthrough he made with his mechanics could salvage something from an otherwise disastrous debut campaign with the team.
Well, in his last eight games, Tucker has batted .414 with seven extra-base knocks, 10 RBIs and more walks (five) than strikeouts (four).
He has hit five home runs in his last 13 games, after collecting just 11 in his first 132 games this year.
It is the version of Tucker that the Dodgers will need in the playoffs, especially with fellow left-handed bats like Shohei Ohtani and Freddie Freeman battling ongoing injuries.
After a season that once seemed so lost, signs of revival have arrived just in time.
PITCHERS OF THE WEEK
Tarik Skubal and Yoshinobu Yamamoto (seven scoreless innings from each)
We are going with a tandem honor this week, from a pair of pitchers who will likely have the biggest influence on the Dodgers' World Series chances.
With Blake Snell battling a groin injury, and Tyler Glasnow entering a Friday start having recently regressed in his return from the injured list, the Dodgers' rotation doesn't feel quite as formidable as it once did.
Then again, if Skubal and Yamamoto keep pitching like they did this week — when they spun consecutive scoreless seven-inning outings in Cincinnati — those other question marks might not feel so daunting.
Both pitchers have sterling postseason track records: Yamamoto with a 7-1 record and 2.25 ERA in 10 playoff outings (including last year's World Series heroics) and Skubal with a 2-1 record and 2.04 ERA in six October appearances of his own (all with the Tigers the last two years).
Either could anchor a pitching staff on their own capable of making a run to the Fall Classic.
Together, they give the Dodgers arguably the best 1-2 punch in the majors. This week, they delivered the club's first pair of back-to-back scoreless seven-inning outings since 2022 when Tyler Anderson and Clayton Kershaw did it.
Granted, dominating the Reds in mid-September is not the same as producing gems in the playoffs.
But with so many other concerns mounting at the moment, Skubal and Yamamoto at least represent a pillar of potential pitching excellence to lean on, one that could compensate for other shortcomings in the Dodgers' three-peat bid.
PROSPECT OF THE WEEK
The entire Dodgers' minor-league system
The Dodgers' big-league club hasn't been the only one popping bottles in beer-soaked clubhouse celebrations recently.
This year, all four of the organization's minor-league affiliates also clinched places in their respective playoffs, with Triple-A Oklahoma City completing the quad-fecta by winning the second-half title in the Pacific Coast League on Wednesday.
It marks the first time the Dodgers have had four affiliates make the playoffs since 2019 (and that year included their now-defunct rookie-ball outpost in Ogden, Utah).
It's also the latest reminder about the strength of depth they boast in their highly touted farm system.
"I know people don't care about minor-league win percentages, but we kind of do," Dodgers general manager Brandon Gomes told the California Post earlier this season. "I think it's a good proxy of how well your farm system is performing and how to understand what it takes to win."
Three of the club's affiliates have already been eliminated, with Double-A Tulsa, High-A Great Lakes and Single-A Ontario all losing in their division championship series.
OKC, meanwhile, will begin its postseason push next week in the best-of-three PCL Championship Series against the Athletics' Las Vegas affiliate. If they win that, they will remain in Vegas for the Triple-A National Championship Game against the winner of the International League.
QUESTION OF THE WEEK
Who should Dodgers hope to see in the first round of the playoffs?
With the NL West crown secured, the Dodgers still have work to do over the season's final nine games.
Given their injury problems, they've never needed a first-round bye so badly.
The good news: They remain four games up on the Braves for the NL's No. 2 seed, with their magic number down to six for securing passage straight to the NL Division Series.
And though they remain two games back of the Brewers for the best record in the majors — and home-field advantage throughout the playoffs — conventional wisdom in recent weeks has suggested that the playoff through the postseason might be better from the 2-seed anyway.
Now, however, the NL playoff field is getting muddied, with the red-hot Padres sitting just one game back of the Cubs and Phillies.
So, who should Dodgers fans root to see in a potential first-round matchup? Well, it depends on what kind of matchup you think suits the Dodgers best.
The Cubs and Phillies had seemed like tougher draws than the Braves or Padres, thanks to Chicago's deep and homer-happy lineup and the Phillies' powerhouse starting rotation trio.
But this week, Philadelphia lost one of its star pitchers, Jesús Luzardo, to a shoulder injury that has put his playoff availability in doubt. The Cubs, meanwhile, have seen their offense cool off and still face questions with an unimposing starting rotation.
The Braves have their own flaws (they've been a middle-of-the-pack offense since the All-Star break) but still boast Chris Sale at the top of their rotation.
The Padres, on the other hand, are making a familiar late-season surge and have a habit of playing the Dodgers tough in the playoffs.
It will all make for a fascinating final few days of scoreboard watching, with a slew of new postseason permutations now on the table.
The Dodgers, of course, won't be overly worried about who they might square off against. Their focus is on continuing to play a better brand of all-around baseball — and making sure they avoid the best-of-three wild-card round.

item.title: [New York Post] Move over, Lakers. Not so fast, Rams. Dodgers are NL West champions again — and still LA’s team
item.dc:creator: Dylan Hernandez

item.content:encoded:
The Dodgers are the National League West champions.
Again.
They have won their division 13 times in the last 14 seasons, and the one time in that period in which they didn’t, they won a then-club-record 106 games.
Somewhere along the way, the Dodgers did the impossible: They met the requirements to become the sports franchise Los Angeles demanded.
Appreciating what this means requires an understanding of how Shaquille O’Neal and Kobe Bryant transformed this city in the early 2000s,
With O’Neal and Bryant as their stars, the Lakers didn’t just win championships.
They were unbeatable.
This image was reinforced by the play of O’Neal, a 7-foot-1, 325-pound freak of nature who literally couldn’t be stopped.
By the time the Lakers completed their three-peat in 2002, championships were no longer something Los Angeles hoped for.
They became something the city expected.
This is the standard used to measure teams with aspirations of becoming a cultural touchstone in this congested market. With plenty of other entertainment options, casual fans won’t invest too much of their time and money in a team unless they believe it will create the kind of citywide pride O’Neal’s Lakers once did.
The Lakers haven’t been that team for some time. The Rams are producing a worthy on-field product, but they remain in the process of winning back fans they lost over the two decades they spent in St. Louis.
The Dodgers are the one team in town that is clearing the bar.
“What’s funny is Los Angeles has always been looked at, as far as sports, (as) a Laker town,” manager Dave Roberts said. “I think we might have the market share right now in Los Angeles. It’s great. I think we draw more fans than anyone in the world, obviously, with the home dates we have. But it’s 40,000, 50,000 every night. We travel well. I do think the guys see it. They feed off it.”
The Dodgers managed to do this despite playing a sport that is particularly hard to dominate. The Lakers could dump the ball into O’Neal 30 times a game. The Dodgers have employed a number of Hall of Famers over the years, but as great as Shohei Ohtani is, he can only hit four times a game, maybe five.
The Dodgers have become a different kind of juggernaut.
With substantial investment from their owners, they have built some of the deepest rosters in baseball history. In its first season operating the team, Guggenheim Baseball Management signed All-Star outfielder Andre Ethier to an $85 million extension, picked up a then-unknown Yasiel Puig for $42 million, traded for All-Star infielder Hanley Ramirez and assumed more than $260 million in contract obligations in a blockbuster trade for Adrian Gonzalez, Carl Crawford and Josh Beckett.
Season after season, the Dodgers fielded one of the most expensive teams in the major leagues — if not the most expensive team.
Which is why at some point in each of the last 14 seasons, the Dodgers were considered favorites to win the World Series.
They are well into their second decade as baseball’s model franchise — or, depending on the perspective, Evil Empire. The last time they didn’t reach the playoffs, the world was a completely different place. LeBron James had just won his first NBA championship. “Gangnam Style” was a global phenomenon. The recreational use of marijuana was still outlawed in every jurisdiction of the United States.
There’s an entire generation of fans who don’t know what it’s like for the Dodgers to not be legitimate contenders.
Consistency by itself didn’t turn the Dodgers into the Dodgers of today. Actually winning championships was important, of course, and doing that required them to adjust how they built their rosters.
President of baseball operations Andrew Friedman used to operate as if the playoffs were a crapshoot. The organization’s focus was on the regular season, on just reaching the postseason. Because depth is required to survive a 162-game schedule, quantity was emphasized over quality.
The approach didn’t produce any championships. The Dodgers reached the World Series twice in their first eight seasons under Guggenheim ownership but lost both times.
The failures prompted them to pursue real difference-makers.
Mookie Betts, who was the catalyst of the championship team in 2020. Freddie Freeman, the home run hero of the 2024 World Series. Yoshinobu Yamamoto, the Most Valuable Player of the 2025 World Series. And, of course, Ohtani, the franchise’s most transformative player since Fernando Valenzuela, or maybe even Jackie Robinson.
The Dodgers have won three of the last six World Series.
Even with Ohtani dealing with right arm and left knee injuries, they will open the postseason as the odds-on favorites to win their third consecutive championship.
As fragmented as Los Angeles can be, most of the city can get behind that.

item.content:encoded:
CINCINNATI — As the celebrating Los Angeles Dodgers drenched one another in various carbonated boozes, the team's most important character was bone dry and most likely quite sober roughly two thousand miles away.
Shohei Ohtani, that baseballing mover of mountains, is injured. A laundry list of ailing body parts — biceps, knee, neck — first kept the two-way dynamo from pitching, then frayed his offensive impact and finally rendered him physically incapable of taking the field. Last week, the Dodgers placed him on the IL, with just a few weeks left for him to recover before the start of the postseason and only five games between his earliest eligible return date and the end of the regular season.
Publicly, the club has maintained an optimistic tone, describing his issues as manageable, not season-ending. A return before the end of the regular season is still in play, skipper Dave Roberts reaffirmed this week. Yet nobody around the game would be shocked if the Dodgers opt for caution and keep Ohtani sidelined until October. Los Angeles' worst-case scenario, of course, would be a postseason without its main man.
So when the Dodgers embarked on their recent two-city swing, their $700 million slugger stayed back in Southern California. He rested, received treatment and hit off a tee — or, as Roberts vaguely put it, "continued his progression."
"Overall, [his] body feels normal-ish," Roberts said before Thursday's clincher. "Then it's kind of getting his body, his knee, his arm, biceps, whatever, back to full strength."
This marked the first time in the Dodgers' Ohtani Era that the man himself did not accompany the team for the entirety of a road trip. In fact, the most recent occurrence of a Dodgers club flying home without Ohtani came in October 2023, after the team's sweep loss to the Diamondbacks in that year's NLDS. Lance Lynn, Austin Barnes and a decade of frustration were on board that plane. Ohtani was still technically an Angel. In other words, it's been a while.
With the two-way superstar now the center of the Dodgers' solar system — and, to a large extent, the league's extended universe — Ohtani's absence this week in Cincinnati was easy to sense, impossible to avoid. Throughout the week, all about the yard, were reminders both big and small.
The blue bat bags lined up outside the locker room in numerical order went right from Will Smith's No. 16 to Kyle Tucker's No. 23, with no No. 17 to be found. Dodgers head security guard Al Garcia, typically within eyesight of Ohtani at all times, floated around the clubhouse with an uncharacteristically laid-back comportment buoyed by his relatively light list of duties.
A group of passionate Dodgers fans recognized the star's absence with a homemade sign that read "Feel Better Shohei, Give Decoy A Hug," making reference to Ohtani's dog. Even Yoshinobu Yamamoto admitted that it was odd not having Ohtani around, delivering one of his funnier and more cutting lines of the season.
"It's been a weird feeling because I talk to him all the time in the clubhouse," Yamamoto said via interpreter Yoshihiro Sonoda. "Although I have Roki [Sasaki], he doesn't really talk to me."
The Dodgers' lineup missed Ohtani, too, averaging less than four runs per game on the road trip before Thursday's eight-run outburst against a bottom-five Cincinnati pitching staff. Utilityman Tommy Edman got the bulk of leadoff duties, with Mookie Betts and rookie call-up Josue De Paula getting a day each in the one-hole. Edman went just 1-for-23 on the trip. Freddie Freeman's power dip continued, with five singles and nothing else. Will Smith has yet to really pop off since his return from the IL on Sept. 1.
"It feels different because he's such a presence when he's on the field," Roberts admitted Monday.
Therein lies the lingering concern. The Dodgers and Ohtani have all but accepted that he won't pitch again this season. That's not the end of the world; Los Angeles has the arms to solve that problem. On the other hand, navigating October without Ohtani at full-go would be a difficult proposition.
Ohtani's health, too, is not binary. Even if he plays, which at this point feels likely, he's unlikely to be completely healed. That dynamic could very well hamper his performance. Ohtani, overly cautious as they come, revealed that concern the last time he spoke to reporters on Sept. 8.
"I should have enough experience to address any kinks or injuries or anything like that with the swing," Ohtani said. "I'm going to use this as an opportunity to add on to the experience that I've had previously and address it regardless."
It's not exactly the most reassuring explanation — Ohtani implying that he'll need to manage his various discomforts for the rest of the season. How that process transpires and how productive Ohtani proves to be in October could determine how many Champagne celebrations he'll get to participate in this year.
